title: चेतना’ एकाङ्कीमा प्रयुक्त लोकविश्वास
nepali: प्रस्तुत लेखमा जयन्ती ‘स्पन्दन’द्वारा लिखित ‘चेतना’ शीर्षकको एकाङ्कीलाई लोकविश्वास दृष्टिले विश्लेषण गरिएको छ । यस अध्ययनमा लोकविश्वासलाई अध्ययनको एउटा महत्वपूर्ण आधारका रूपमा लिइएको छ । लोकविश्वास लोकजीवनसँग जोडिएको हुन्छ । अझ भनौँ लोकविश्वास नै लोकजीवनको मियो हो । यो शब्द ‘शकुन’सँग सम्बन्धित भएकाले प्राचीन समयमा लोकविश्वासलाई शकुन पनि भनिन्थ्यो । ‘शकुन’ शब्दले लोकले विश्वास गर्ने शुभाशुभ सन्दर्भलाई सङ्केत गर्दछ तथापि सबै लोकविश्वास सकारात्मक अर्थका मात्र देखिँदैनन् । कतिपय नकारात्मक प्रकृतिका लोकविश्वास लोकजीवनमा रहेका छन् । यस्तै मानव शरीर, खाना, मानवेतर शरीर, यात्रा, व्यवहार, सपना, आदिसँग सम्बन्धित लोकविश्वास नेपाली लोकजीवनमा विद्यमान देखिन्छन् । यस लेखमा यिनै लोकविश्वासका आधारमा ‘चेतना’ एकाङ्कीको अध्ययन र विश्लेषण गरिएको छ । प्रस्तुत एकाङ्कीमा धर्म र संस्कृतिसँग सम्बन्धित लोकविश्वासले लोकजीवनमा बढी प्रभाव पारेको र त्यसले नकारात्मक अर्थका साथ लैङ्गिक असमानतालाई बढावा दिएको यथार्थसँग साक्षात्कार गराउँदै समाज रूपान्तरका लागि यस्ता लोकविश्वास लोकजीवनमा अन्त्य हुनुपर्ने क्रान्तिकारी वैचारिकी अनिवार्यताको निष्कर्ष निकालिएको छ ।
american_english: The present paper analyzes the one-act play titled 'Chetna', written by Jayanti 'Spandan', from the perspective of folk belief. In this study folk belief has been taken as an important basis for the study. Folk belief is bound up with folk life. To put it even more strongly, folk belief is itself the core of folk life. Because this word is connected with 'shakun' (omen), in ancient times folk belief was also called shakun. The word 'shakun' points to the auspicious and inauspicious matters that people believe in; however, not all folk beliefs are seen in a positive sense alone. Some folk beliefs of a negative nature are present in folk life. Likewise, folk beliefs connected with the human body, food, non-human bodies, travel, behavior, dreams and so on are seen to exist in Nepali folk life. In this article, on the basis of these very folk beliefs, the study and analysis of the one-act play 'Chetna' has been carried out. In the present one-act play, the revolutionary ideology that such folk beliefs must come to an end in folk life for the sake of social transformation has been arrived at as an unavoidable conclusion, as it confronts the reality that folk beliefs connected with religion and culture have had a greater influence on folk life and that they have promoted gender inequality in a negative sense.
british_english: This paper analyses the one-act play entitled 'Chetna', written by Jayanti 'Spandan', from the standpoint of folk belief. In the present study, folk belief has been taken as an important basis for the investigation. Folk belief is bound up with the life of the folk. Indeed, folk belief is the very core of folk life. Since this word is related to 'shakun' (omen), in ancient times folk belief was also called shakun. The term 'shakun' signifies the auspicious and inauspicious references in which the folk believe; nonetheless, not all folk beliefs are encountered in a positive sense only. Certain folk beliefs of a negative character are to be found in folk life. In the same way, folk beliefs connected with the human body, food, non-human bodies, travel, conduct, dreams and the like are observed to exist in Nepali folk life. In this article, on the strength of these very folk beliefs, the study and analysis of the one-act play 'Chetna' has been undertaken. In the one-act play before us, the revolutionary ideology that such folk beliefs must be brought to an end in folk life for the sake of social transformation has been drawn as an unavoidable conclusion, as it confronts the reality that folk beliefs connected with religion and culture have had a greater impact upon folk life and that they have encouraged gender inequality in a negative sense.
australian_english: This paper takes the one-act play titled 'Chetna', written by Jayanti 'Spandan', and examines it through the lens of folk belief. In this study, folk belief has been taken as an important basis for the work. Folk belief is tied up with folk life. Put more bluntly, folk belief is the very hub of folk life. Because the word is linked with 'shakun' (omen), in ancient times folk belief was called shakun as well. The word 'shakun' points to the lucky and unlucky matters that people believe in; even so, not every folk belief turns up in a positive light. Some folk beliefs of a negative bent remain in folk life. In the same way, folk beliefs having to do with the human body, food, non-human bodies, travel, behaviour, dreams and the like are found in Nepali folk life. In this article, working from these same folk beliefs, the study and analysis of the one-act play 'Chetna' has been done. In the one-act play at hand, the revolutionary thinking that such folk beliefs must be finished off in folk life if society is to be transformed has been arrived at as an unavoidable conclusion, as it squares up to the reality that folk beliefs bound up with religion and culture have had a bigger influence on folk life and have pushed gender inequality in a negative way.
informal_english: This paper takes 'Chetna', the one-acter written by Jayanti 'Spandan', and has a look at it through the lens of folk belief. In this study, folk belief is treated as one of the main starting points. Folk belief goes hand in hand with folk life. To put it even more plainly, folk belief is the very hub of folk life. The word is tied up with 'shakun' (an omen), so in the old days folk belief got called shakun too. The word 'shakun' points to the lucky and unlucky things people put their faith in; but it's not the case that every folk belief is a positive one. A few folk beliefs of a negative kind are still hanging around in folk life. And the same goes for folk beliefs to do with the human body, food, non-human bodies, travel, how people behave, dreams and so on — all of these turn up in Nepali folk life. In this article, working from these very folk beliefs, the study and analysis of the one-act play 'Chetna' has been done. In the play in front of us, the revolutionary idea that this sort of folk belief has to come to an end in folk life if society is going to change has been arrived at as something you can't really argue with, given that it squares up to the reality that folk beliefs tied to religion and culture have had a bigger say in folk life and have pushed gender inequality in a bad way.
translator_notes: Abstract translated sentence by sentence in source order; 'lokvishwas' rendered as 'folk belief' throughout and 'shakun' kept in transliteration with a gloss on first use; one-act title 'Chetna' transliterated as it appears in the abstract.
